newsitem.title: Australia: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: PEARSON APOLOGISES TO HIS PEOPLE FOR 1993 BLUNDER
Aboriginal lawyer, Noel Pearson, says he and other Aboriginal leaders were political fools for advocating a peace offering in 1993 over negotiations on Native Title.

Mr Pearson told a National Trust Forum in Brisbane, that it was the biggest strategic blunder to offer validation of title since 1975 in order to receive graciousness from the other side. Mr Pearson says tens of thousands of pastoralists and mining companies have taken advantage of the offer, and are now demanding extinguishment of native title.
Mr Pearson apologised to his people for the strategic blunder.
NATIONAL CODE OF PRACTICE FOR BUILDING INDUSTRY
Federal Industrial Relations Minister, Peter Reith, says an agreement reached today with the states, for the Building and Construction Industry, could lead to more jobs and greater efficiency.
The Ministers have adopted industrial relations standards for the National Code of Practice, to be released in August.

Under the agreement, union closed shops will be banned on government construction projects, with governments also agreeing not to allow employers to be pressured into making over-award payments to employees.
On government projects, unions or employers won't be allowed to pressure or coerce the other into starting, varying or terminating workplace agreements.
Unions also won't be allowed to force employers to pay superannuation into union-dictated funds.
And the code bans discrimination on the grounds of union or non-union membership.
Mr Reith says he hopes the private sector also will voluntarily adopt the code.
KATTER SAYS ABORIGINAL CHILDREN SITLL BEING REMOVED
North Queensland National Party backbencher, Bob Katter, says during his time as a State MP in the early 1990s, Aboriginal children were still being forcibly removed from their families.
The member for Kennedy says he's aware of several cases where up to five children from one family have been taken from their parents for no apparent reason.
Mr Katter says that in his reckoning, he was handling a case every three weeks from an electorate of 20,000 people, describing the problem as horrific.
FEDERAL GOVT OFFERS STATES EXTRA CASH FOR DISABILITY SERVICES
The Federal Government's offered the states and territories an extra $25 million in funding for disability services.
Minister for Disability Services Judy Moylan announced the extra funding at an a meeting of State and Territory Ministers in Canberra today.
Mrs Moylan says the 25-million dollars comes on top of 54-million dollars contained in the budget.
She's hopeful her offer will break a deadlock on funding that led to peak disability body, ACROD, sending a letter to members warning them of retrenchments and cuts to services.
FORMER TASMANIAN CRICKET CAPTAIN CONVICTED FOR THEFT
A court has been told a former Tasmanian Sheffield Shield cricket captain was too proud to declare himself bankrupt and began stealing from his employer.
Roland Shane Hyatt, aged 35, has been given a nine-month suspended jail sentence after admitting stealing thousands of dollars from a Hobart fitness club to pay his debts and feed a gambling habit.
But, the court heard Hyatt has been on a downward spiral since he lost his wife, his high-paying job and developed a large debt problem, after his wife gave birth to a still-born child six years ago.
Hyatt was the Tasmanian cricket captain for six years and played 30 games for the state.
CHILD CARE SUMMIT IN CANBERRA
A warning today that the Federal Government's budget cuts to child care can expect some strong opposition when the measures go before the Senate.
More than one-hundred parents and child-care workers are attending a child care summit at Parliament House in Canberra, organised by ACT Labor Senators Kate Lundy and Annette Ellis.
Senator Lundy says fee increases of up to 40-dollars a week, resulting from the cut to child-care places and subsidies, means many families can no longer afford to work.
LABOR SAYS PM APOLOGY IN PARLIAMENT WON'T LEAD TO LIABILITY
The Federal Opposition says the Prime Minister can officially apologise to the Stolen Generation, without it being used in any court proceeding.
Mr Howard says an unqualified formal apology for the forcible removal of Aboriginal children from their families, could open up the question of compensation.
But Shadow Attorney General, Nick Bolkus, says the same legal advice the Government used to block a Senate Inquiry into Mal Colston, means the Government can apologise.
Senator Bolkus says the advice from the Government's Chief General Counsel, Henry Burmeister, was that statements made in Parliament can't be used in subsequent legal proceedings.
-- Sydney Newroom 61-2 9373-1800
